A* : comme Dijkstra, mais il ajoute une: A*: like Dijkstra, but it adds an estimate of the remaining distance (Manhattan). It heads for the goal and visits far fewer cells, for the same path.
BFS : explore en cercles autour du dépar: BFS: explores in circles around the start, layer by layer. Finds the shortest path in number of cells, but ignores mud.
Ce plugin doit être approuvé par NeoDex: This plugin must be approved by NeoDex to open.
Cherche le plus petit élément du reste e: Finds the smallest element of the rest and puts it in front. Always the same number of comparisons, but very few swaps.
Choisit un pivot, met les plus petits à: Picks a pivot, puts the smaller ones on the left and the bigger ones on the right, then starts over on each side. The most used in practice; slow on an already sorted array with this pivot choice (the last one).
Compare chaque paire de voisins et les é: Compares each pair of neighbours and swaps them if they are out of order: big ones rise to the end like bubbles. Simple, but slow.
Coupe le tableau en deux, trie chaque mo: Cuts the array in two, sorts each half (by starting over), then merges the two sorted halves. Always fast, but it needs extra room.
DFS : fonce dans une direction tant qu'i: DFS: rushes in one direction as long as it can, and only backs up when stuck. Finds a path, rarely the shortest.
Dijkstra (1956) : explore toujours la ca: Dijkstra (1956): always explores the cheapest cell from the start. It takes mud into account (cost 5) and finds the cheapest path.
L'algorithme choisi, la vitesse et la gr: The chosen algorithm, the speed and the drawn grid.
Les deux tris rangent le même tableau, u: Both sorts work on the same array, one step (a comparison or a write) each at a time. The first one to finish wins.
Même tableau, une étape chacun à la fois: Same array, one step each at a time.
Ne compare jamais : compte combien de fo: Never compares: counts how many times each value appears, then rewrites the array in order. Unbeatable when the values are small integers.
O(n log n) en moyenne, O(n²) au pire: O(n log n) on average, O(n²) at worst
No path: the goal is walled in.
Prend chaque élément et le glisse à sa p: Takes each element and slides it into place among the ones already sorted, like arranging cards in your hand. Very fast on a nearly sorted array.
Range le tableau en tas (chaque parent p: Arranges the array as a heap (each parent bigger than its children), moves the root (the biggest) to the end, repairs the heap, and starts over.
Regarde les algorithmes travailler, étap: Watch algorithms work, step by step: 8 sorts (bubble, insertion, selection, merge, quick, heap, Shell, counting), 2 searches (linear, binary) and 4 graph traversals on a grid you draw (breadth-first, depth-first, Dijkstra, A*) with walls, mud and mazes. The pseudo-code lights up line by line, comparisons and writes are counted, and you step forward, back or change the speed at will. New: a race between two sorts on the same array.
Regarde les cases une par une jusqu'à tr: Looks at the cells one by one until it finds it. Works even if the array is not sorted.
Sur un tableau trié : regarde le milieu,: On a sorted array: looks at the middle, and throws away the half where the value can't be. 1000 cells? 10 looks are enough.
Un tri par insertion sur des éléments él: An insertion sort on far-apart elements (gap n/2, then n/4…), which quickly brings elements close to their place, then a last pass with gap 1.
